title: The return the pension fund assumes, and the return it earned
question: The size of the pension bill depends on the investment return the fund assumes. How often did it earn that much?
finding: The fund earned less than the return it assumed in 5 of the 11 years to June 2025. Over the whole period it earned 8.0% a year on average against 7.4% assumed; that average leans on one year, 2021, when it earned 35.4%, and without it the other 10 years average 5.6%. The worst year was 2022 (-6.2%). The assumed return was cut from 7.50% to 7.20% over the period.
how: Actual return is the “money-weighted rate of return” in the pension note of each year’s audited statements. Assumed return is the rate the same note says was used to measure what the fund owes at that June 30; the actuary’s separate accounting reports print the same rate in every year they cover. The averages are compound averages of the yearly figures.
limits: Investment returns swing from year to year, and a fund is expected to miss its assumption in many single years; what matters is the long-run average, which here is above the assumption only because of one exceptional year. An assumption being missed is not misconduct. A lower assumed return makes the promised pensions look larger and the required contributions higher.
